c-lang: In C, given int a[] = {10, 20, 30}; int *p = a; what is the value of *(p + 2)?
It does not compile
p + 2 points to the third element, a[2], because pointer arithmetic counts in elements, not bytes.
In C, if int *p holds address 1000 and sizeof(int) is 4, what address does p + 1 hold?
Adding 1 to a pointer advances it by one element, which is sizeof(int) = 4 bytes here.
What is the key difference between malloc(n * sizeof(int)) and calloc(n, sizeof(int)) in C?
calloc zero-fills the block; malloc leaves it uninitialized
malloc zero-fills the block; calloc leaves it uninitialized
calloc allocates on the stack; malloc allocates on the heap
calloc memory is freed automatically; malloc memory is not
calloc initializes every byte to zero (and checks the n * size multiplication for overflow); malloc returns uninitialized memory.
A C program does p = realloc(p, new_size); What is the problem with this line?
On failure it returns NULL and the old block is leaked
realloc cannot enlarge a block, so new_size is ignored
realloc clears the old data, so the contents are lost
realloc allocates on the stack, so p dies at return
If realloc fails it returns NULL but leaves the original block allocated. Assigning the result straight to p loses the only pointer to it. Use a temporary pointer.
What does free(NULL) do in standard C?
Nothing; it is a valid no-op
It crashes with a segmentation fault
It is undefined behavior
It returns an error code
The C standard says that if the argument to free is a null pointer, no action occurs.
Assuming int is 4 bytes, what is sizeof(union { int i; char c[4]; }) on a typical compiler?
All members of a union share the same storage, so its size is that of the largest member (plus any alignment padding), here 4.
On a typical x86-64 compiler (4-byte int, default alignment), what is sizeof(struct { char c; int i; })?
The compiler inserts 3 bytes of padding after c so that i is 4-byte aligned: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8.
A C function contains char buf[16]; ... return buf; What happens when the caller uses the returned pointer?
Undefined behavior, because buf no longer exists
It works, because arrays are copied on return
It works, because buf is moved to the heap
Compilation fails with a type mismatch error
buf has automatic storage on the stack and its lifetime ends when the function returns, so the pointer dangles. Compilers usually warn but still compile it.
Where does a non-static local variable declared inside a C function typically live?
On the stack (automatic storage)
On the heap (dynamic storage)
In the data segment (static storage)
In the read-only text segment
Local variables without static have automatic storage duration, which implementations place in the function's stack frame.
Which call reads a line into char buf[64] in C without risking a buffer overflow?
fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin)
gets(buf)
scanf("%s", buf)
fscanf(stdin, "%s", buf)
fgets writes at most sizeof buf - 1 characters plus the terminator. gets was removed in C11, and %s without a width has no limit.
Which C declaration makes f a pointer to a function that takes two ints and returns an int?
int (*f)(int, int);
int *f(int, int);
int (*f)(int);
(int *) f(int, int);
The parentheses bind * to f, so f is a pointer. Without them, int *f(int, int) declares a function returning int *.
What comparator signature does the C standard library function qsort expect?
int (*)(const void *, const void *)
bool (*)(const void *, const void *)
int (*)(void *, void *, size_t)
void (*)(const void *, const void *)
qsort calls the comparator with pointers to two elements and expects a negative, zero or positive int result.
Given #define SQUARE(x) x * x in C, what does SQUARE(1 + 2) evaluate to?
The macro expands textually to 1 + 2 * 1 + 2 = 5. Writing ((x) * (x)) fixes it.
What is the purpose of #ifndef MY_H / #define MY_H / #endif around a C header's contents?
It prevents the header from being included twice in one file
It makes the header's functions inline by default
It hides the header's symbols from other source files
It speeds up linking by skipping unused functions
Include guards stop repeated definitions when the same header is pulled in more than once into a translation unit.
What does printf return in C when it succeeds?
The number of characters written
The number of arguments it formatted
Zero to indicate success
A pointer to the output buffer
printf returns the count of characters transmitted, or a negative value if an output error occurs.
Which printf format specifier is correct for a value of type size_t (C99 and later)?
%zu
%d
%lu
%u
The z length modifier denotes size_t. %lu happens to work on some platforms but is not portable, for example on 64-bit Windows.
In C, int x = INT_MAX; x = x + 1; What does the standard say about the result?
It is undefined behavior
It is guaranteed to wrap to INT_MIN
It is guaranteed to become 0
It is guaranteed to stay at INT_MAX
Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior. Only unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap around modulo 2^N.
In C, what does the statement i = i++ + 1; do?
It is undefined behavior
It increments i by exactly 1
It increments i by exactly 2
It leaves i unchanged
i is modified twice without a sequencing rule between the modifications, which is undefined behavior; compilers may produce any result.
What is the value of (5 & 3) | (1 << 3) in C?
Which C statement clears bit 3 of an unsigned int x and leaves the other bits unchanged?
ANDing with a mask that has only bit 3 at zero clears it. |= sets the bit, ^= toggles it, and &= with the plain mask clears every other bit.
cpp: What does RAII mean in C++?
A resource is tied to an object and released in its destructor
Resources are allocated once at compile time and reused
A garbage collector releases resources when memory is low
Resources are acquired lazily the first time they are used
Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: the constructor acquires the resource and the destructor releases it, so cleanup happens on every exit path.
Why is std::lock_guard<std::mutex> preferred over calling m.lock() and m.unlock() by hand?
It unlocks in its destructor, even when an exception is thrown
It makes the mutex faster by skipping kernel calls
It lets several threads hold the same mutex at once
It detects deadlocks and throws an exception instead
lock_guard is an RAII wrapper: leaving the scope, normally or via an exception, runs the destructor, which releases the lock.
In C++, auto a = std::make_unique<int>(5); std::unique_ptr<int> b = a; What happens?
Compilation fails, because unique_ptr cannot be copied
b and a now share ownership of the same int
b gets a deep copy of the int with value 5
a is silently moved into b and set to null
unique_ptr's copy constructor is deleted to keep single ownership. Use std::unique_ptr<int> b = std::move(a); to transfer it.
In C++, after std::unique_ptr<int> b = std::move(a); what does a hold?
nullptr
The same pointer as b
A dangling pointer to freed memory
A copy of the original int
Moving a unique_ptr transfers ownership and the standard guarantees the source is left empty (equal to nullptr).
Two C++ objects hold std::shared_ptr references to each other and nothing else refers to them. What happens?
Neither is destroyed, because each keeps the other's count above 0
Both are destroyed when the last outside pointer goes away
The program throws std::bad_weak_ptr when the scope ends
The runtime detects the cycle and frees the older object
Reference counting cannot reclaim cycles. Making one of the links a std::weak_ptr breaks the cycle.
In C++, how do you safely use the object behind a std::weak_ptr<T> w?
Call w.lock() and check the returned shared_ptr
Dereference w directly with *w
Call w.get() and check for null
Cast w to a raw pointer with static_cast
lock() atomically returns a shared_ptr that keeps the object alive, or an empty one if it has already been destroyed. weak_ptr has no operator* or get().
What does std::move(x) actually do in C++?
It casts x to an rvalue reference so a move can be chosen
It moves the bytes of x to a new memory location
It destroys x and returns a new copy of its value
It swaps x with a default-constructed object
std::move is just a cast to T&&. The actual move happens only if a move constructor or move assignment is selected.
Why should a C++ class's move constructor be marked noexcept?
std::vector reallocation uses it only if it cannot throw
The compiler refuses to call a move constructor otherwise
noexcept makes the moved-from object automatically empty
It allows the move constructor to be called at compile time
To keep the strong exception guarantee, vector moves elements during reallocation only if the move cannot throw (or no copy is available); otherwise it copies.
Given template<typename T> T maxOf(T a, T b); what happens with the call maxOf(3, 4.5)?
Compilation fails: T is deduced as both int and double
T is deduced as double and 4.5 is returned
T is deduced as int and 4 is returned
T is deduced as auto and the call works
Template argument deduction requires both deductions to agree. Fix it with maxOf<double>(3, 4.5) or by using two type parameters.
In C++, Base* p = new Derived; p->f(); where f is NOT virtual in Base and Derived defines its own f. Which f runs?
Base::f
Derived::f
Both, Base::f first
The call is ambiguous and fails
Without virtual, the call is bound statically using the pointer's static type, Base.
In C++, a class used polymorphically has no virtual destructor, and code runs delete p; where Base* p points to a Derived. What is the result?
Undefined behavior; Derived's destructor may never run
Derived's destructor runs, then Base's destructor
Only Base's destructor runs, which is well defined
The compiler rejects the delete expression
Deleting a derived object through a base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behavior. Declare virtual ~Base() in polymorphic bases.
In C++, std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 2, 3}; std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 2); What is v.size() afterwards?
std::remove only shifts kept elements forward and returns the new logical end; it cannot change the container size. Follow it with v.erase(it, v.end()).
You need a C++ container mapping string keys to values with average O(1) lookup and no ordering requirement. Which fits best?
std::unordered_map
std::map
std::list
std::set
unordered_map is a hash table with average constant-time lookup. std::map is a balanced tree with O(log n) lookup and sorted keys.
In C++, a loop holds an iterator it into std::vector v and calls v.push_back(x) inside the loop. What is the risk?
Reallocation can invalidate it, so using it is undefined
push_back throws if any iterator is still active
it automatically moves to point at the new element
The new element is skipped, but it stays valid
If push_back exceeds capacity, the vector reallocates and all iterators, pointers and references to its elements become invalid.
In C++, what does the declaration const int* p mean?
p cannot modify the int it points to, but p can be repointed
p cannot be repointed, but it can modify the int
Neither p nor the int it points to can change
p points to an int that must be a compile-time constant
const before * applies to the pointee. int* const p would make the pointer itself constant.
Why is catch (const std::exception& e) preferred over catch (std::exception e) in C++?
It avoids copying and slicing the derived exception
It catches exceptions from other threads as well
It lets the handler modify and rethrow the copy
It is required for catching standard exceptions
Catching by value copies the object and slices off derived parts, so e.what() may lose the derived message. A reference keeps the real type.
In C++11 and later, what happens if an exception escapes a destructor that has no explicit noexcept(false)?
std::terminate is called
The exception propagates to the caller normally
The exception is silently discarded
The object is destroyed a second time
Destructors are implicitly noexcept since C++11, so an escaping exception calls std::terminate.
Under the C++ rule of five, a class defines a destructor, copy constructor and copy assignment. Which two members complete the set?
Move constructor and move assignment operator
Default constructor and conversion operator
Swap function and comparison operator
Virtual destructor and clone method
The rule of five adds the move constructor and move assignment, since user-declared copy operations or a destructor suppress the implicit moves.
A C++ class owns a raw pointer, deletes it in the destructor, and relies on the compiler-generated copy constructor. What happens after copying an object?
Both copies delete the same pointer, a double free
The copy gets its own new allocation automatically
The compiler refuses to generate a copy constructor
Only the original deletes the pointer at scope exit
The default copy constructor copies the pointer value (shallow copy). This is why the rule of three exists; the rule of zero avoids it with std::unique_ptr or containers.
On x86-64 (8-byte double with 8-byte alignment), what is sizeof(struct { char a; double b; char c; })?
a takes 1 byte plus 7 padding so b is aligned, b takes 8, c takes 1 plus 7 tail padding: 24. Reordering to double b; char a; char c; shrinks it to 16.
rust: In Rust, let s1 = String::from("hi"); let s2 = s1; println!("{}", s1); What happens?
Compile error: borrow of moved value s1
It prints hi, because s2 is a copy of s1
It prints an empty string
It panics at runtime with a use-after-move
String is not Copy, so let s2 = s1 moves ownership to s2 and s1 can no longer be used. The check happens at compile time.
In Rust, let a: i32 = 5; let b = a; println!("{}", a); What happens?
It prints 5, because i32 implements Copy
Compile error, because a was moved into b
It prints 0, because a was reset by the move
It panics, because a is no longer valid
Simple scalar types like i32 implement Copy, so assignment copies the value and a stays usable.
Which statement correctly describes Rust's borrowing rules for a value at any one time?
Either one mutable reference or any number of shared ones
Any number of mutable references, but only one shared
One mutable and one shared reference at the same time
Any mix of references, checked only at runtime
The borrow checker enforces aliasing XOR mutability: many &T, or exactly one &mut T, and references must not outlive the value.
In Rust, let mut v = vec![1]; let first = &v[0]; v.push(2); println!("{}", first); Why does this fail to compile?
v is borrowed mutably while first still borrows it
vec! macros cannot be modified after creation
first must be declared with let mut
push requires v to be passed by value
push needs &mut v, but the shared borrow first is still used afterwards. This prevents first from dangling if push reallocates.
Why does fn longest(x: &str, y: &str) -> &str { ... } fail to compile in Rust?
The return lifetime cannot be inferred from two inputs
Functions cannot return references in Rust
&str arguments must be passed as String
The function body must use unsafe code
With two reference inputs, elision rules cannot pick one. Writing fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str ties them together.
What is the type of the string literal "hello" in Rust?
&'static str
String
&mut str
Box<str>
String literals are stored in the binary and live for the whole program, so they are &'static str. String is an owned heap type.
In Rust, what does fn show<T>(x: T) where T: Clone + Debug require of T?
T must implement both Clone and Debug
T must implement Clone or Debug
T must be a struct deriving Clone
T must be a reference type
A + in a trait bound combines bounds, so the type must satisfy all of them.
Can a Rust crate write impl std::fmt::Display for Vec<i32>?
No, because both the trait and type are foreign
Yes, any crate can implement any trait
Yes, but only inside an unsafe block
No, because Vec has no fields to print
The orphan rule requires the trait or the type to be local to the crate. The usual workaround is a newtype like struct MyVec(Vec<i32>).
In Rust, enum Color { Red, Green, Blue } and a match on a Color with arms only for Red and Green. What happens?
Compile error: the match is not exhaustive
Blue silently falls through to the Green arm
It panics at runtime only when Blue is matched
It compiles with an unreachable pattern warning
match must cover every possible value. Add a Blue arm or a wildcard _ arm.
In Rust, what does match x { 1 | 2 => "small", 3..=5 => "mid", _ => "big" } evaluate to when x is 5?
"mid"
"big"
"small"
It fails to compile
3..=5 is an inclusive range pattern, so 5 matches it. The _ arm would catch anything above 5.
In a Rust function returning Result<T, E>, what does let v = parse(s)?; do?
Returns early with the converted Err, or unwraps Ok into v
Panics on Err, or unwraps Ok into v
Converts Err into None and stores it in v
Retries parse(s) until it returns Ok
The ? operator propagates the error to the caller, converting it via From, and evaluates to the Ok value otherwise.
What does Some(3).map(|x| x * 2).unwrap_or(0) evaluate to in Rust?
Some(6)
map transforms the inner value to Some(6), and unwrap_or returns the inner value 6 because it is Some.
You need several Rust threads to share read-only ownership of one value. Which smart pointer fits?
Arc<T>
Rc<T>
Box<T>
RefCell<T>
Arc uses atomic reference counting and is Send and Sync when T is. Rc is not thread-safe, Box has one owner, and RefCell gives no sharing.
In Rust, let c = RefCell::new(5); let a = c.borrow_mut(); let b = c.borrow_mut(); What happens?
It panics at runtime with a borrow error
Compile error from the borrow checker
Both a and b get mutable access
b silently waits until a is dropped
RefCell moves borrow checking to runtime. A second active mutable borrow panics (try_borrow_mut returns an Err instead).
Why does enum List { Cons(i32, Box<List>), Nil } need the Box in Rust?
It gives the recursive type a known, finite size
It makes List automatically thread-safe
It allows List to be mutated through &self
It enables reference counting of the nodes
Without indirection the type would contain itself and have infinite size. Box is a pointer with a fixed size.
Why does std::thread::spawn(move || println!("{}", rc)) fail to compile when rc is an Rc<i32>?
Rc<i32> is not Send, so it cannot move to another thread
Closures passed to spawn cannot capture variables
i32 values cannot be printed from other threads
spawn requires the closure to return a Result
Rc's reference count is not atomic, so Rc does not implement Send. Arc is the thread-safe alternative.
Which Rust type is the standard choice for a counter that several threads increment?
Arc<Mutex<i32>>
Rc<RefCell<i32>>
Box<Cell<i32>>
&mut i32 shared by all
Arc shares ownership across threads and Mutex provides synchronized mutable access. Rc and RefCell are single-threaded. (An AtomicI32 in an Arc also works.)
What does the ! in vec![1, 2, 3] indicate in Rust?
A macro invocation
An unsafe function call
A call that may panic
A logical negation
Names followed by ! are macros, such as vec!, println! and format!. Macros expand to code at compile time.
Which Rust operation requires an unsafe block?
Dereferencing a raw pointer
Creating a raw pointer with as *const i32
Calling a method on a Box
Indexing a Vec with []
Creating a raw pointer is safe; reading or writing through it is not, because the compiler cannot verify it is valid.
Where does cargo build --release place the compiled binary by default?
target/release/
target/debug/
bin/release/
build/out/
Cargo builds into target/debug by default and into target/release with the release profile, which enables optimizations.
zig: In idiomatic Zig, how does a library function that needs heap memory usually obtain it?
It takes a std.mem.Allocator parameter
It calls a global default heap allocator
It reads a thread-local allocator setting
It uses the C malloc function implicitly
Zig has no hidden global allocator. Passing an Allocator makes allocation explicit and lets the caller choose the strategy.
A Zig server makes many small allocations per request and can free them all when the request ends. Which allocator fits best?
std.heap.ArenaAllocator
std.heap.page_allocator alone
std.testing.allocator in production
No allocator, using global variables
An arena hands out memory from a child allocator and frees everything at once with deinit(), so individual frees are unnecessary.
In Zig, which call releases const buf = try allocator.alloc(u8, 100);?
allocator.free(buf)
allocator.destroy(buf)
std.c.free(buf)
buf.deinit()
Memory from alloc (a slice) is released with free. destroy is the counterpart of create, which allocates a single item.
What happens in Zig when allocator.alloc cannot obtain memory?
It returns error.OutOfMemory
It returns a null slice
It aborts the program
It throws an exception
Allocation failure is an ordinary error value that the caller must handle, for example with try or catch.
In Zig, what does the parameter declaration comptime T: type in fn max(comptime T: type, a: T, b: T) T mean?
T must be known at compile time
T is inferred at runtime from a and b
T is erased after type checking
T must be a pointer type
comptime parameters are evaluated during compilation. Passing types this way is how Zig writes generic functions.
How are generic data structures such as a typed list usually written in Zig?
A function takes a comptime type and returns a type
Through template blocks like in C++
Through runtime type tags on each element
Through a special generic keyword on struct
For example, fn List(comptime T: type) type { return struct { items: []T }; }. Types are first-class values at compile time.
In Zig, why does a ++ b fail when a and b are slices whose lengths are only known at runtime?
++ requires operands with comptime-known lengths
++ is defined only for numeric types
++ needs both operands to be mutable
++ only works inside a defer block
++ concatenates arrays at compile time. Runtime concatenation needs an allocator, for example std.mem.concat.
In a Zig function returning !void, what does try foo() do?
Returns foo's error to the caller, or yields its value
Retries foo until it succeeds
Converts the error into a panic
Ignores the error and continues
try x is shorthand for x catch |err| return err. On success it evaluates to the payload.
In Zig, what does const n = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, s, 10) catch 0; do?
Uses 0 if parsing returns an error
Returns 0 from the current function
Panics with the code 0 on failure
Retries parsing with base 0
catch provides a fallback value when the left side is an error. The surrounding function continues normally.
When does a Zig errdefer statement run?
Only when the scope exits by returning an error
On every scope exit, like defer
Only when the program panics
Only at the end of the program
errdefer is used for cleanup that should happen only on failure, such as freeing a partially built object.
In Zig, a line foo(); calls a function returning !void and does not use the result. What happens?
Compilation fails because the error is ignored
The error is silently discarded at runtime
The program panics if foo returns an error
A warning is printed and execution continues
Zig refuses to compile code that ignores an error union. Handle it with try, catch or if.
Which feature does Zig deliberately leave out to keep "no hidden control flow"?
Operator overloading
The defer statement
Inline functions
Compile-time evaluation
Without operator overloading (or exceptions), an expression like a + b can never call a function behind the reader's back.
In Zig, how do you add two u8 values so that 255 + 1 wraps to 0?
Use the +% operator
Use + in a ReleaseSafe build
Use the ++ operator
Cast both values to i8 first
+% is wrapping addition. Plain + is checked: overflow panics in Debug and ReleaseSafe builds and is undefined in ReleaseFast.
What does declaring a Zig type as extern struct guarantee?
Its fields follow the C ABI layout
It must be defined in a C header
Its fields may be reordered freely
It is always allocated on the heap
Plain Zig structs have no guaranteed layout. extern struct uses C-compatible field order and padding for interop.
What is zig cc commonly used for?
As a drop-in C compiler with easy cross-compilation
As a converter from C source to Zig source
As a linter for Zig code style
As the Zig package registry client
zig cc wraps Clang and ships libc headers for many targets, so it can compile C for other platforms without extra toolchains.
In a Zig project, what is build.zig?
A Zig source file that defines the build, run by zig build
A JSON file listing compiler flags
A Makefile that zig build converts
A lock file of resolved package versions
The build is described in Zig itself. Package dependencies are declared separately in build.zig.zon.
What does running zig test math.zig do?
Compiles the file and runs its test blocks
Formats the file and reports style issues
Builds a release binary named test
Checks the file for syntax errors only
Blocks like test "add" { try std.testing.expect(add(1, 2) == 3); } are collected and run by zig test.
In Zig, const arr = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }; const s = arr[1..3]; What does s contain?
2 and 3
1, 2 and 3
2, 3 and 4
1 and 2
Slicing uses a half-open range [start..end), so indexes 1 and 2 are included.
In a Zig Debug build, what happens when code indexes a slice past its length?
The program panics with an index out of bounds error
It reads whatever memory lies after the slice
The index wraps around to the start
The slice grows to fit the index
Safety checks are on in Debug and ReleaseSafe. In ReleaseFast they are removed and the access is undefined behavior.
In Zig, a function body contains defer print("a"); defer print("b"); What is printed when the function returns?
b then a
a then b
Only b
Only a
Deferred statements run in reverse order of declaration when the scope exits.
fortran: In Fortran, real :: a(10) is declared with no explicit bounds. Which indexes are valid?
1 to 10
0 to 9
0 to 10
1 to 9
Fortran arrays start at index 1 by default, unlike C.
Fortran stores arrays in column-major order. For real :: a(3, 4), which element comes right after a(1, 1) in memory?
In column-major order the first index varies fastest, so for speed the innermost loop should run over the first index.
In Fortran, what is size(b) for integer :: b(-2:2)?
Bounds -2:2 are inclusive, giving the indexes -2, -1, 0, 1 and 2.
In Fortran, integer :: v(5) = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. What is sum(v(2:4))?
The section v(2:4) contains v(2), v(3) and v(4), which are 2, 3 and 4.
How many times does the body of the Fortran loop do i = 1, 10, 3 execute?
i takes the values 1, 4, 7 and 10. The upper bound is inclusive when the step lands on it.
How many times does the body of the Fortran loop do i = 10, 1 execute?
The default step is +1, so the iteration count max((1 - 10 + 1) / 1, 0) is zero. A countdown needs do i = 10, 1, -1.
Inside a Fortran DO loop, which statement skips the rest of the current iteration and starts the next one?
cycle
exit
continue
next
cycle is like continue in C, while exit leaves the loop like break. In Fortran, CONTINUE is a no-op statement.
What is the main benefit of placing Fortran subroutines inside a module and accessing them with use?
Calls get an explicit interface, so arguments are checked
The subroutines run in parallel automatically
The subroutines no longer need a call statement
Module variables are stored in double precision
Module procedures have explicit interfaces, so the compiler checks argument count, type and rank at each call. Old external procedures had none.
A Fortran subroutine declares real, intent(in) :: x and then executes x = 2.0. What happens?
The compiler reports an error
The caller's variable becomes 2.0
A local copy of x is changed
The value is ignored at runtime
intent(in) means the dummy argument must not be redefined, and compilers diagnose the assignment at compile time.
In Fortran, real :: a(3, 4). What does shape(a) return?
shape returns a rank-1 array of the extents along each dimension. size(a) would give 12 and rank(a) would give 2.
What do the Fortran intrinsics mod(-7, 3) and modulo(-7, 3) return?
-1 and 2
2 and -1
-1 and -1
2 and 2
mod uses truncation, taking the sign of the first argument. modulo uses floor, taking the sign of the second argument.
Which Fortran declaration portably requests a real with at least 15 significant decimal digits?
real(selected_real_kind(15)) :: x
real(kind=15) :: x
real*15 :: x
real(precision=15) :: x
Kind numbers are compiler-specific, so selected_real_kind(15) (or real64 from iso_fortran_env) is the portable choice.
In Fortran, x is declared real(real64) and the code does x = 0.1. What precision does x end up with?
Single precision, because 0.1 is a default real constant
Double precision, because x is declared as real64
Quad precision, because the constant is promoted
It depends on the loop that uses x later
The literal 0.1 is default (usually 32-bit) real and is rounded before conversion. Write 0.1_real64 or 0.1d0 to keep full precision.
In Coarray Fortran, integer :: x[*] is declared. What does x[3] refer to?
The copy of x on image 3
The third element of x
x on every image except 3
x copied 3 times locally
Square brackets are codimensions: each image has its own x, and x[3] accesses the one on image 3.
In Coarray Fortran, what does the statement sync all do?
Waits until every image reaches this point
Copies all coarrays to image 1
Ends execution on all images
Starts all images in parallel
sync all is a barrier across all images, often used before reading data another image has written.
A Fortran file contains !$omp parallel do before a loop and is compiled without OpenMP enabled. What happens?
The directive is treated as a comment
Compilation fails with an error
The loop runs in parallel anyway
The loop body is skipped
OpenMP directives start with the !$omp sentinel, which looks like a comment to a compiler without OpenMP support, so the code stays serial.
A Fortran OpenMP loop adds values into a shared variable s and gives wrong totals. Which clause fixes it?
reduction(+:s)
private(s)
shared(s)
nowait
reduction gives each thread a private copy of s and combines them at the end, removing the data race. private(s) would discard the results.
In legacy Fortran without implicit none, an undeclared variable named kount is used. What type does it get?
integer
real
character
logical
By default, names starting with I through N are integer and all others are real. implicit none turns this off.
In fixed-form FORTRAN 77 source, what does a non-blank character in column 6 mean?
The line continues the previous statement
The line is a comment
The line carries a statement label
The line is a compiler directive
Columns 1 to 5 hold labels, column 6 marks continuation and statements go in columns 7 to 72. A C or * in column 1 marks a comment.
Which Fortran standard first made coarrays part of the language?
Fortran 2008
Fortran 90
Fortran 95
Fortran 77
Coarrays were added in Fortran 2008 and extended with teams and events in Fortran 2018.
assembly: In the System V AMD64 ABI (Linux, macOS), which register holds a function's integer return value?
RAX
RDI
RBX
RSP
Integer and pointer results are returned in RAX (with RDX for the upper half of 128-bit values).
Which x86-64 register holds the address of the next instruction to execute?
RIP
RSP
RBP
RSI
RIP is the instruction pointer. RSP is the stack pointer and RBP is often the frame pointer.
On x86-64, RAX holds 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF and the code runs mov eax, 1. What is RAX afterwards?
0xFFFFFFFF00000001
0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFF01
Writing a 32-bit register zero-extends into the full 64-bit register. Writing AL or AX leaves the upper bits unchanged.
What is a key difference between ARM and x86 as instruction set architectures?
ARM is load/store; x86 allows memory operands in ALU ops
x86 is load/store; ARM allows memory operands in ALU ops
ARM has no general-purpose registers at all
x86 has no instructions for accessing memory
On ARM, arithmetic works only on registers and memory is accessed through loads and stores. x86 can do add rax, [rbx] directly.
How long are AArch64 (A64) instructions compared with x86-64 instructions?
A64 uses a fixed 32 bits; x86-64 varies from 1 to 15 bytes
Both use a fixed length of 32 bits
A64 varies from 1 to 15 bytes; x86-64 uses 32 bits
Both vary from 2 to 8 bytes
Fixed-length encoding simplifies decoding on ARM, while x86 uses variable-length instructions with prefixes.
On AArch64, where does the BL instruction store the return address?
In X30, the link register
On the stack at [SP]
In X0, the first argument register
In the program counter PC
BL writes the return address to X30 (LR) and branches. A function that calls others must save LR before its own BL.
In Intel syntax, what does mov rax, [rbx + rcx*8 + 16] load into RAX?
8 bytes from address rbx + rcx*8 + 16
The value rbx + rcx*8 + 16 itself
8 bytes from address rbx, then adds 16
16 bytes starting at rbx + rcx*8
Brackets mean a memory access with base + index*scale + displacement addressing, often used for array element access.
What does lea rax, [rbx + 8] do on x86-64?
Sets RAX to RBX + 8 without reading memory
Loads 8 bytes from address RBX + 8 into RAX
Stores RAX at address RBX + 8
Adds 8 to RBX and copies it into RAX
lea computes the effective address only. It is often used for cheap arithmetic like rax = rbx + rcx*4 + 8. RBX is not modified.
In Intel syntax, what does mov eax, [0x1000] put into EAX?
The 4 bytes stored at address 0x1000
The number 0x1000
The address of EAX
The 4 bytes at the address held in 0x1000
Square brackets denote a memory operand (direct addressing). mov eax, 0x1000 without brackets would load the immediate value.
Under the System V AMD64 calling convention, which register carries the first integer argument?
RDI
RAX
RCX
RSP
The first six integer arguments go in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8 and R9. Windows x64 uses RCX, RDX, R8 and R9 instead.
What does the x86-64 call instruction do?
Pushes the return address and jumps to the target
Jumps to the target without saving anything
Saves all registers and jumps to the target
Pushes RBP and sets RBP to RSP
call pushes the address of the next instruction onto the stack, and ret pops it back into RIP.
Under the System V AMD64 ABI, which register must a function preserve for its caller (callee-saved)?
RBX
RAX
RCX
RDI
RBX, RBP, RSP and R12 to R15 are callee-saved. RAX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI and R8 to R11 may be clobbered.
Under the System V AMD64 ABI, what alignment must RSP have right before a call instruction?
16 bytes
4 bytes
8 bytes
32 bytes
RSP must be a multiple of 16 at the call, so on entry RSP + 8 is 16-byte aligned. Misalignment can crash SSE code such as printf.
On Linux x86-64, which register holds the system call number for the syscall instruction?
RAX
RDI
RBX
The number goes in RAX, arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, R10, R8 and R9, and the result comes back in RAX.
On Linux x86-64, which register carries the fourth argument of a system call?
RCX
R8
RDX
Normal functions use RCX for the fourth argument, but the syscall instruction overwrites RCX with the return address, so the kernel uses R10.
What distinguishes a hardware interrupt from a system call?
A device raises it asynchronously, not the running code
The running code raises it with a special instruction
It can only happen while the CPU is in user mode
It is handled entirely in user space
A system call is a deliberate, synchronous request by the program. Hardware interrupts arrive at any time and the CPU runs a handler in the kernel.
What does cmp eax, ebx do on x86?
Computes eax - ebx, sets flags, and discards the result
Computes eax - ebx and stores it in eax
Copies ebx into eax if they differ
Swaps eax and ebx if eax is larger
cmp is a subtraction that only updates flags such as ZF, SF, CF and OF, which conditional jumps then test.
On x86, AL holds 0x7F and the code runs add al, 1. Which flags describe the result?
OF = 1 and CF = 0
OF = 0 and CF = 1
OF = 1 and CF = 1
OF = 0 and CF = 0
0x7F + 1 = 0x80: as signed bytes 127 + 1 overflows to -128 (OF set), but as unsigned bytes 127 + 1 = 128 fits, so no carry.
After cmp eax, ebx, which x86 jump is taken if EAX is greater than EBX when both are treated as unsigned?
ja
jg
jl
jb
ja (jump if above) uses CF and ZF for unsigned comparisons. jg (jump if greater) is the signed version.
On x86, what does the sequence test eax, eax followed by jz done do?
Jumps to done if EAX is zero
Jumps to done if EAX is negative
Jumps to done if EAX is nonzero
Jumps to done unconditionally
test ANDs EAX with itself and sets ZF when the result is zero. jz (same as je) jumps when ZF is set.
verilog: In Verilog-2001, what kind of signal must appear on the left side of an assign statement?
A net, such as a wire
A reg variable
An integer variable
A parameter
Continuous assignments drive nets. Variables like reg are assigned in procedural blocks. (SystemVerilog relaxes this with logic.)
Which Verilog statement describes a tri-state buffer that drives a onto y only when en is 1?
assign y = en ? a : 1'bz;
assign y = en ? a : 1'b0;
assign y = en & a;
assign y = en ? a : 1'bx;
z is the high-impedance value, which lets other drivers control the line. Driving 0 or x would conflict with them.
In Verilog-2001, how must q be declared if it is assigned inside always @(posedge clk)?
As reg q
As wire q
As parameter q
As supply0 q
Signals assigned procedurally must be variables (reg). Note that reg does not always mean a flip-flop; that depends on the logic.
Why is always @(*) preferred for combinational logic in Verilog?
It includes every signal read in the block automatically
It makes the block run on every clock edge
It forces the block to use non-blocking assignments
It turns the block into a testbench process
A hand-written sensitivity list that misses a signal causes a mismatch between simulation and synthesized hardware.
What does always @(*) if (en) q = d; synthesize to in Verilog?
A latch, because q keeps its value when en is 0
A flip-flop clocked by en
Pure combinational wiring from d to q
A tri-state buffer controlled by en
When en is 0 there is no assignment, so q must hold its value, which requires a latch. Add an else or a default assignment.
In a Verilog always @(posedge clk) block, a <= b; b <= a; runs on a clock edge. What happens?
a and b swap values
Both get the old value of b
Both get the old value of a
Only a changes
Non-blocking assignments read all right-hand sides first and update together at the end of the time step.
In a Verilog always @(posedge clk) block, a = b; b = a; runs on a clock edge. What happens?
Both end up with the old value of b
a and b swap values
Both end up with the old value of a
Neither changes
Blocking assignments execute in order: a takes b first, then b takes the new a, which is the old b.
What is the standard Verilog guideline for choosing between = and <=?
Use <= in clocked blocks and = in combinational blocks
Use = in clocked blocks and <= in combinational blocks
Use <= everywhere, since = is deprecated
Use = everywhere, since <= is only for simulation
Following this rule avoids race conditions between clocked blocks and keeps simulation consistent with synthesized hardware.
A Verilog designer writes always @(posedge clk) begin q1 = d; q2 = q1; end intending a 2-stage shift register. What is built?
One stage: q1 and q2 both take d at each edge
A correct 2-stage shift register
A latch on q2 controlled by q1
No logic, since q2 is unused
With blocking assignments q2 reads the new q1, which is already d. Using q1 <= d; q2 <= q1; gives two stages.
What is the main advantage of named port connections like adder u1 (.a(x), .b(y), .sum(s)); in Verilog?
They do not depend on the order of ports
They make the instance simulate faster
They allow connecting ports of any width
They create copies of the module
Named association stays correct if the module's port order changes and makes mismatches easier to spot.
How do you instantiate a Verilog module counter with its WIDTH parameter set to 8?
counter #(.WIDTH(8)) c1 (...);
counter c1 #(.WIDTH(8)) (...);
counter c1 (.WIDTH = 8, ...);
counter<8> c1 (...);
Parameter overrides come between the module name and the instance name, using #( ... ).
Where can a module instance appear in Verilog?
In a module body, outside procedural blocks
Inside an always block, under a condition
Inside an initial block in a testbench
Inside a function or task body
Instances describe structural hardware and are not executable statements, so they cannot be placed in always, initial, functions or tasks.
What is typical of a Verilog testbench top module?
It has no ports and drives the design from initial blocks
It must be synthesizable into hardware
It has the same ports as the design under test
It contains only continuous assignments
A testbench wraps the design, generates stimulus and checks results in simulation only.
In a Verilog testbench, how does $monitor differ from $display?
$monitor prints whenever one of its arguments changes
$monitor prints once at the end of simulation
$monitor prints only when an error occurs
$monitor writes to a waveform file
$display prints once when executed. $monitor keeps watching its arguments and prints each time one changes.
With `timescale 1ns/1ps in Verilog, what does #5 mean?
A delay of 5 ns
A delay of 5 ps
A delay of 5 clock cycles
A delay of 1 ns, rounded to 5 ps
The first value sets the time unit for delays and the second sets the rounding precision.
In a Verilog testbench with initial clk = 0; and always #5 clk = ~clk; what is the clock period?
10 time units
5 time units
20 time units
2.5 time units
The clock toggles every 5 units, so one full cycle (high then low) takes 10.
A Verilog testbench declares reg clk; and uses always #5 clk = ~clk; with no initial value. What does clk do?
It stays at x for the whole simulation
It toggles normally starting from 0
It toggles normally starting from 1
It stays at z for the whole simulation
A reg starts as x, and ~x is still x. Initialize it with initial clk = 0;.
In FSM design, what distinguishes a Moore machine from a Mealy machine?
Moore outputs depend only on the current state
Moore outputs depend on state and current inputs
Moore machines have no state register
Moore machines cannot have a reset
Mealy outputs also depend on inputs, so they can react within the same cycle but may produce glitches.
In Verilog, what does always @(posedge clk or posedge rst) indicate for an FSM state register?
An asynchronous, active-high reset
A synchronous, active-high reset
A clock that runs on both edges
A reset that is only used in simulation
Listing rst in the sensitivity list lets it change the state immediately, without waiting for a clock edge.
How many flip-flops does a 5-state FSM need with binary encoding and with one-hot encoding?
3 and 5
5 and 3
3 and 3
5 and 32
Binary needs ceil(log2 5) = 3 bits. One-hot uses one flip-flop per state, which often simplifies next-state logic on FPGAs.
vhdl: In VHDL, what is the role of an entity compared with an architecture?
The entity declares the ports; the architecture its behavior
The entity holds the behavior; the architecture the ports
The entity is a testbench; the architecture is the design
The entity lists libraries; the architecture lists signals
The entity is the external interface, and an architecture body describes how the design works inside.
How many architectures can one VHDL entity have?
One or more, and a configuration or binding picks one
Exactly one, defined in the same file
Zero, since architectures replace entities
Exactly two: one behavioral, one structural
An entity can have several architectures, such as a behavioral model and a structural one. By default the most recently analyzed one is used.
In VHDL-93, an architecture reads the value of a port declared with mode out. What happens?
It is a compile error; VHDL-2008 allows reading it
It always reads 'U' in simulation
It reads the value from the previous clock
It works the same in all VHDL versions
Before VHDL-2008, out ports could not be read inside the architecture, so designers used an internal signal or mode buffer.
What is the key difference between a VHDL signal and a variable inside a process?
A variable updates at once; a signal after the process suspends
A signal updates at once; a variable after the process suspends
Both update at once, in program order
Both update only at the next clock edge
Variable assignment (:=) takes effect immediately. Signal assignment (<=) is scheduled and visible after a delta cycle.
Inside one VHDL process, s <= '0'; is followed by s <= '1';. What value does s get?
Within a process, a later signal assignment overrides an earlier one, so the last assignment wins. Separate concurrent drivers would resolve to 'X'.
Where are VHDL variables (other than shared variables) declared?
In the declarative part of a process or subprogram
In the entity's port list
In the architecture's declarative part
In the library clause
Ordinary variables are local to a process, function or procedure. Signals are declared in the architecture.
A combinational VHDL process is written as process(a) but also reads b. What is the effect?
Simulation misses changes on b, unlike the hardware
Synthesis fails with a missing signal error
b is treated as a constant zero
The process runs on every delta cycle
The process wakes only on a. Synthesis usually ignores the list and builds logic using b, so simulation and hardware disagree.
What does process(all) mean in VHDL-2008?
The process is sensitive to every signal it reads
The process runs once at time zero
The process drives every signal in the design
The process waits on all clocks in the design
process(all) removes the risk of incomplete sensitivity lists in combinational logic.
What happens in simulation to a VHDL process that has neither a sensitivity list nor any wait statement?
It loops forever at time zero and the simulation hangs
It runs once and then stops for good
It runs once on every clock edge
It is removed by the simulator
A process repeats from the top when it ends, and only a wait (or a sensitivity list) can suspend it.
Why is rising_edge(clk) preferred over clk'event and clk = '1' in VHDL?
It ignores transitions such as 'X' to '1'
It runs faster in synthesized hardware
It also detects falling edges
It is required for asynchronous reset
rising_edge is true only for a real '0' to '1' transition (including 'L' and 'H' forms), so simulation of unknown values is more accurate.
In a VHDL architecture body, two concurrent signal assignments appear outside any process. Does their order matter?
No, both describe hardware that is active in parallel
Yes, the first one is evaluated first
Yes, the last one overrides the first
Only if they drive different signals
Concurrent statements execute whenever their inputs change, regardless of their position in the code.
In VHDL-93, which statement can appear directly in an architecture body outside any process?
y <= a when sel = '1' else b;
if sel = '1' then y <= a; else y <= b; end if;
case sel is when '1' => y <= a; when others => y <= b; end case;
for i in 0 to 3 loop y(i) <= a(i); end loop;
when/else is a concurrent conditional assignment. if, case and loop statements are sequential and belong inside a process.
Which VHDL construct is the concurrent counterpart of a case statement?
with sel select y <= ...;
if ... elsif ... end if;
wait until sel'event;
loop ... exit when sel;
A selected signal assignment chooses a value based on one expression, like case does inside a process.
What is a VHDL generic, such as generic (WIDTH : integer := 8)?
A constant parameter set when the entity is instantiated
A signal shared by all entities in the design
A variable that changes during simulation
A library that defines generic data types
Generics parameterize an entity, for example bus width, and can be overridden per instance with a generic map.
How do you override the WIDTH generic of a counter instance in VHDL?
u1: entity work.counter generic map (WIDTH => 16) port map (...);
u1: entity work.counter port map (WIDTH => 16, ...);
u1: entity work.counter (WIDTH => 16) port map (...);
u1: entity work.counter generic (WIDTH := 16) port map (...);
Generic values are given in a generic map placed before the port map.
What does u1: and2 port map (a => x, b => y, c => z); use for connecting ports in VHDL?
Named association, mapping formal ports to actual signals
Positional association, by order of declaration
Generic association, with constant values
Implicit association, by matching signal names
formal => actual connects each port by name, so the order of the list does not matter.
What does direct entity instantiation, u1: entity work.and2 port map (...);, avoid in VHDL-93?
The need for a separate component declaration
The need for a port map
The need to compile the entity first
The need for a library clause for ieee
Component instantiation requires a matching component declaration; direct entity instantiation refers to the compiled entity in a library.
What is the initial simulation value of a std_logic signal declared without a default value?
Signals start with the leftmost value of their type, and std_logic begins with 'U' (uninitialized).
Two VHDL drivers put '0' and '1' on the same std_logic signal at the same time. What is the resolved value?
std_logic is a resolved type, and a conflict between strong 0 and strong 1 resolves to 'X'. std_ulogic does not allow multiple drivers.
Which IEEE package is the recommended way to do arithmetic on vectors in VHDL?
ieee.numeric_std with signed and unsigned
ieee.std_logic_arith with std_logic_vector
ieee.math_real with real values
std.textio with string values
numeric_std is the IEEE standard package. std_logic_arith is a non-standard vendor package that can conflict with it.
